acts.title: Text A · What the phrase actually means
text: The Internet of Things is the technology which allows a physical object — a fridge, a smoke alarm, a car — to communicate with other objects or with people.

People have been talking about smart fridges for twenty years, so the reasonable question is what has changed. The answer is price. Microchips, which used to be expensive, can now be manufactured for almost nothing, and anything that carries one can be put online.
It is estimated that there are between ten and fifteen billion things connected to the internet, compared with only two billion people who are.

The examples that are usually given are domestic. A heating system that accesses the GPS in your phone can turn itself on when you are twenty minutes away. A washing machine whose inbuilt computer detects a fault can look up repair companies and book itself in.

The example that matters most is not domestic at all. An insulin pump which is attached to the body monitors blood levels, injects when necessary, and sends the readings to a doctor, who can then monitor a patient remotely.

items.q: What does the text say has changed recently?
o: Microchips have become cheap enough to put in anything

items.q: Which example does the writer say matters most?
o: The insulin pump that lets a doctor monitor a patient remotely

acts.title: Text B · The three worries, in order of seriousness
text: The first worry, which almost everybody raises, is what happens when it fails. Anybody who is heavily dependent on connected devices has a problem the moment the Wi-Fi does.
The second is privacy. The question that people actually ask is not who collects the data — that is usually stated somewhere — but who it is later sold to, and for what.

The third is security, and it is the one that changes as the objects change. A computer that is hacked is expensive. A fridge that is hacked is embarrassing. A car whose brakes are online, or an insulin pump which is attached to somebody’s body, is a different category of problem altogether.

There is a fourth worry, which is mentioned less often and may in the end be the largest: the amount of storage all this data requires. The people whose broadband slows down as a result will not know why.

items.s: The first worry the writer names is what happens when the connection fails.
The writer says the main privacy question is who collects the data.
The writer treats a hacked car differently from a hacked fridge.
The fourth worry is about the amount of storage required.
The writer thinks the fourth worry is the least important.

text: The technology which allows a physical object to communicate with people.

The examples that are usually given are domestic.

items.q: “The technology which allows an object to communicate…” — what does the clause do?
o: It identifies which technology — you cannot remove it

items.q: “Microchips, which used to be expensive, can now be made cheaply.” Remove the clause. What happens?
o: The sentence still makes complete sense

items.q: What is the difference in punctuation between the two?
o: The extra-information clause has commas; the identifying one does not

items.q: “a machine whose inbuilt computer…” — what does whose mean here?

acts.title: Relative clauses: essential or extra
rule: A relative clause adds information to a noun. Everything about the grammar follows from one question: does the reader need that information in order to know which one you mean? If yes, it is defining and takes no commas. If no, it is non-defining and takes commas on both sides.
points: No commas. Use who, which or that. The information identifies the noun and cannot be removed.
Commas on both sides. Use who or which — never that. The information is extra.
Possession, for people and for things alike: a machine whose computer detects a fault.
Only in a defining clause, and only when it is the object: the tablet you gave me.
Every device can be hacked, which is the real worry. Here which refers to the whole idea.
the town where I grew up; the year when it opened.
eg: The man who lives above me plays loud music.
Defining — it says which man.
John, who lives next door, has a smart fridge.
Non-defining — we already know who John is.
Cars which are internet-connected can book their own service.
Defining — only those cars.
My car, which is internet-connected, books its own service.
Non-defining — I have only one car.
The woman whose desk is next to mine is on holiday.
whose, for a person.
A machine whose computer detects a fault can call for help.
whose, for a thing.
The tablet you gave me is really useful.
Object pronoun left out — defining only.
Every device can be hacked, which is the real worry.
which referring to the whole clause.
This is the town where I grew up.
where, for a place.
1900, when the Métro opened, was a good year for Paris.
when, non-defining.
acts.careful: “My car, that is internet-connected, books its own service” is wrong. that is never used in a non-defining clause, and a non-defining clause always needs its commas.

use: the thing that worries me is…

write.q: Write about 180 words on the connected devices in your own life — what you have, what you would never install, and why. Use at least three defining relative clauses without commas, at least two non-defining clauses with commas, one whose, and one which referring back to a whole idea.
plan: what you have, and what each one does
one thing you are unsure about
write.model:
The connected things I own are unremarkable: a phone, a router which is older than it should be, and a heating controller that I installed in 2021 and have adjusted perhaps four times.

The controller, which cost about the same as a month’s gas, has probably saved me nothing. What it did do was tell me that the flat above mine is heated to twenty-six degrees, which explains a great deal about my own bills.

What I would not install is a camera. I know somebody whose doorbell records every person who walks past the building, and he does not think of it as surveillance because he does not watch it. Somebody does.

The one I am unsure about is the water meter, which the building is installing this spring whether anybody agrees or not. The thing that worries me is not the meter. It is that nobody has said who reads the data, or for how long it is kept.
